podcast.title: "Female Elvis Presley"
podcast.body: Wanda Jackson was known as the "female Elvis Presley" due to her powerful voice and pioneering rockabilly style. She garnered significant admiration from notable musicians, including Jack White, who is a big fan of her work. "There was one to Jackson, otherwise known as the female Elba's Pressley."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Female Elvis Presley"
podcast.body: Wanda Jackson, a country guitarist, was sometimes referred to as the "female Elvis Presley." "sometimes called the female Elvis Presley."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Childhood Musical Aspirations
podcast.body: Before even starting school, Wanda Jackson was deeply influenced by Rose Maddox's stage presence and decided she wanted to be a "girl singer just like Rose Maddox." Her father supported this ambition, buying her a guitar from the Sears Robuck catalogue when she was six and teaching her chords. They would play together nightly, with her mother writing down chords for songs they learned from radio and records.

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 43: "I Gotta Know" by Wanda Jackson

podcast.title: Discovery of Elvis Presley and Influence
podcast.body: After leaving school and becoming a full-time musician, Jackson's father, her manager, secured a booking agent named Bob Neal in Memphis. Neal arranged for her to tour with a new singer he managed, Elvis Presley, and Johnny Cash. Backstage at the first show, she heard the "terrible screaming" from Elvis's fans and immediately recognized he was not an ordinary country singer. They started dating, and Elvis gave her his ring, which she still possesses. He had a profound influence on her, teaching her to strum an acoustic guitar with a single strum, a more rock and roll style, and convincing her to pursue rockabilly music.

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 43: "I Gotta Know" by Wanda Jackson

podcast.title: Early Life and Migration
podcast.body: Born in Oklahoma, Wanda Jackson and her family migrated to California during the tail end of the Great Depression, as "stragglers in the Great Migration" of "Oak Ease." They lived in Greenfield, a few miles from Bakersfield, where her father worked. This put her in the same musical and social environment as future Bakersfield Sound musicians, before they moved back to Oklahoma a few years later.

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 43: "I Gotta Know" by Wanda Jackson

podcast.title: Early TV Show and Mentorship (14 years old)
podcast.body: At 14, after auditioning for a local TV show, Hank Thompson discovered Wanda Jackson. Initially unaware of her age due to her mature voice, he invited her to perform with his band. Although she had never played with a band and felt she wasn't good initially, Thompson mentored her, teaching her stage performance and eventually inviting her to his local TV show, which led to her getting her own show in Oklahoma.

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 43: "I Gotta Know" by Wanda Jackson

podcast.title: Exposure to Western Music (Ages 5-10)
podcast.body: Due to her parents' inability to afford babysitters, Wanda Jackson frequently accompanied them to dances on weekends, where she saw "almost every great western band of the 40s." This early exposure shaped her musical tastes and aspirations, leading her to admire artists like Spade Cooley and The Maddox Brothers and Rose.

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 43: "I Gotta Know" by Wanda Jackson

podcast.title: Father's Disapproval of Elvis
podcast.body: Wanda Jackson's father, who managed her, was unimpressed with Elvis Presley's stage performance, criticizing his energetic movements and vocal style. Despite his reservations, Elvis profoundly influenced Wanda's musical direction.

podcast.title: Female Elvis Presley
podcast.body: Wanda Jackson was known by the moniker "the female Elvis Presley" and is a significant figure in rock and roll history, with musician Jack White expressing admiration for her work. "There was one to Jackson, otherwise known as the female Elvis Presley. Jack White is a big fan of her."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Grand Ole Opry Scandal (Uncovered Shoulders)
podcast.body: During her first performance at the Grand Ole Opry, Wanda Jackson was told she could not go on stage in her chosen dress because her shoulders were uncovered, which was deemed "obscene" by the establishment. At the time, she was one of the only country singers trying to present a glamorous image rather than a "farm girl" look. When she complied by wearing a jacket, she was further humiliated by comedy acts who mocked her throughout her set, confirming the country establishment's resistance to her style.

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 43: "I Gotta Know" by Wanda Jackson

podcast.title: Japan Success
podcast.body: Despite facing difficulties with chart success in the United States, Wanda Jackson achieved her biggest success overseas in Japan. She became a significant rock and roll star there, an early example of an artist finding fame abroad before achieving it in their home country.

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 43: "I Gotta Know" by Wanda Jackson

podcast.title: Producer Missteps
podcast.body: After the relative failure of "Hot Dog! That Made Him Mad," producer Ken Nelson struggled to find suitable material for Wanda Jackson at Capitol Records. While her own rockabilly tracks often lacked the power of her live shows, Nelson's choices were particularly poor, leading to records that failed commercially, such as the Calypso-influenced "Don't Wanna."

podcast.title: Recorded at Owen Bradley's Studio
podcast.body: Wanda Jackson recorded at Owen Bradley's studio in Nashville when she was in the city, rather than in Los Angeles. "and where Wanda Jackson recorded when she was in Nashville rather than LA."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Rejection by Capitol Records (Underage)
podcast.body: While Wanda Jackson was still in high school, Hank Thompson recorded demos of her singing and presented them to Ken Nelson at Capitol Records. Nelson liked her voice but declined to sign her due to her being under 18, citing legal complications and the fact that she hadn't finished school.

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Self-Taught Yodeling
podcast.body: Wanda Jackson taught herself to yodel by copying Alton Britt's record "Chime Bells," a skill that was essential for country and western singers at the time, dating back to Jimmie Rodgers.

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Touring with Jerry Lee Lewis
podcast.body: Wanda Jackson toured with Jerry Lee Lewis, Johnny Cash, and Carl Perkins, an experience where Lewis quickly overshadowed his fellow acts despite not yet having a hit. "Jerry Lee went out on tour with Johnny Cash, Carl Perkins, Wanda Jackson and a couple of other acts."
